H1.text: A closed bottle of water never dries up. An open glass dries up in days.

H2.text: A soda bottle stays calm until you open it. Then it fizzes.

H3.text: Diya drops ice into water in her kitchen. Ice and water sit side by side. Nothing seems to change.

H4.text: Last time we asked: at equilibrium, does everything really stop?

H5.text: By the end, you will see that nothing stops. Two changes run at the same speed, both ways.

P1.text: Think of a shop with one door.

P2.text: Every minute, five people walk in. Every minute, five people walk out.

P3.text: The crowd inside stays the same. But the people keep changing.

P4.text: Not stopped, but balanced. This is dynamic equilibrium. Dynamic means always moving.

S1.text: Let's put ice and water on our molecule bench, in a closed flask at zero degrees Celsius.

S2.text: Some molecules break free from the ice and join the water. That is melting.

S3.text: At the same time, some water molecules stick back onto the ice. That is freezing.

S4.text: Count them. Melting, five each second. Freezing, five each second. Equal.

S5.text: So the amount of ice stays the same, and so does the amount of water.

S6.text: This happens at two seventy three kelvin, at normal air pressure. That is the normal melting point.

L1.text: Next, water and its vapour. Vapour means the gas form of water.

L2.text: In a closed box, molecules escape into the space above. That is evaporation.

L3.text: As vapour builds up, some molecules hit the water and come back. That is condensation.

L4.text: Soon both speeds are equal. The level stops dropping, and the vapour pressure stays fixed.

L5.text: In an open glass, the vapour drifts away for good. No balance, so it dries up.

L6.text: Water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius at one point oh one three bar. That is its normal boiling point.

D1.text: Some solids turn straight into vapour. This is sublimation.

D2.text: Iodine, camphor and ammonium chloride do this. In a closed jar, both ways run at equal speeds.

D3.text: Now keep adding sugar to water until no more dissolves. The solution is saturated.

D4.text: Has dissolving stopped? Scientists added sugar with a radioactive tag, a marker they can track.

D5.text: The tag soon showed up in the solution and in the solid. Sugar keeps dissolving and coming back.

G1.text: Now gases in liquids. Why does soda fizz when you open it?

G2.text: In a sealed bottle, carbon dioxide sits above the drink at high pressure. Gas goes in and out at equal speeds.

G3.text: Henry's law: the mass of gas that dissolves is proportional to the gas pressure above the liquid. Double the pressure, double the gas.

G4.text: Open the cap. The pressure falls, so the extra gas bubbles out. Fizz.

G5.text: Warm the drink, and even less gas stays dissolved. Warm soda goes flat faster.

C1.text: Compare. A closed bottle: molecules escape and return at equal speeds. An open glass: they escape and never return.

K1.text: Pause and think. Can an open glass of water ever reach equilibrium?

K2.text: No. Equilibrium needs a closed system, so the vapour cannot escape.

R1.text: Now the rules every physical equilibrium follows.

R2.text: One. It happens only in a closed system, at a fixed temperature.

R3.text: Two. Both opposite changes go on at the same speed.

R4.text: Three. Things we can measure, like pressure and amount, stay constant.

R5.text: Four. Each has one fixed value at a given temperature, like the vapour pressure.

R6.text: Five. The size of that value tells us how far the change has gone.

T1.text: Remember this. Equilibrium does not mean stopped. It means balanced.

W2.text: A drink holds one point five grams of carbon dioxide per litre at one bar. At the same temperature, it is sealed at four bar. How much dissolves?

W3.text: Henry's law. The mass dissolved is proportional to the pressure.

W4.text: The pressure became four times bigger. Four bar divided by one bar is four.

W5.text: So the mass is four times one point five. Six grams per litre.

W6.text: Open the cap, back to about one bar. Only one point five grams can stay. Four and a half grams fizz out.

X2.text: Students write: at equilibrium, melting and freezing have stopped.

X3.text: Wrong. Both go on, at equal speeds. Only the overall change is zero.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Boards ask for the characteristics and Henry's law. Entrance tests ask which statement is true.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Water and its vapour are at equilibrium in a closed vessel. Which statement is correct? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. The vapour pressure stays constant at a given temperature.

A2.text: Evaporation and condensation both go on at equal speeds. So A is wrong.

A3.text: Vapour pressure depends on the temperature, not on how much water is there. So C is wrong.

A4.text: An open vessel lets the vapour escape. So D is wrong.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. What does dynamic equilibrium mean?

Y3.text: Two. Why can an open glass of water never reach equilibrium?

Y4.text: Three. Why does soda fizz when you open the bottle?

N1.text: Next time: does a chemical reaction also keep running both ways? We find out in Equilibrium in Chemical Processes.
